title: Adjectives
intro: Adjectives describe nouns. Learn the order of adjectives, the -ed and -ing pairs and comparisons at B1, then gradable adjectives and stronger comparisons at B2.

sources.label: British Council: Gradable and non-gradable adjectives

sections.title: Order of adjectives
sections.summary: When you use more than one adjective before a noun, the order is usually fixed.
uses: Put opinion adjectives first, then fact adjectives: a nice big house.
Size, age, shape, colour, origin and material follow in that order.
Use no more than two or three adjectives together.
Do not use and between adjectives before a noun, but use and between the last two after be: The room is big, bright and clean.

examples.text: She wore a beautiful long red dress.
He bought a small old wooden boat.
The room is warm and comfortable.
examples.note: After the verb be you can use and.

mistakes.why: Do not use and before the noun.

sections.title: Adjectives ending in -ed and -ing
sections.summary: -ed adjectives describe how a person feels. -ing adjectives describe the thing or person that causes the feeling.

tables.caption: Pairs of adjectives
head: feeling (-ed)
cause (-ing)
example
rows: I am bored. The film is boring.
She is interested in art. Art is interesting.
I am tired. The journey was tiring.
We are excited. The match is exciting.
He was surprised. The news was surprising.

uses: Use -ed for the person who has the feeling: I am confused.
Use -ing for the thing or person that makes the feeling: The instructions are confusing.
Other pairs: amazed/amazing, annoyed/annoying, disappointed/disappointing, frightened/frightening, worried/worrying.

examples.text: I was shocked by the news.
I find maths difficult but interesting.

mistakes.wrong: I am boring in this lesson.
mistakes.right: I am bored in this lesson.
mistakes.why: I feel bored. If you say boring, you mean that you make others bored.
The trip causes the feeling, so use -ing.

checks.question: Choose: I am (worried / worrying) about the test.
checks.explanation: This is the feeling of a person.

sections.title: Comparatives and superlatives
sections.summary: Use comparatives to compare two things and superlatives to say which is first in a group.
uses: Use one-syllable adjectives + -er / -est.
Use more / most with adjectives of three or more syllables and many of two syllables: more modern, most careful.
Use than after a comparative: My brother is older than me.
Use the before a superlative: the highest mountain.
Equal comparison: as tall as. Not equal: not as tall as.
A double comparative shows a change: It gets colder and colder.

examples.text: This is the most interesting book I have read.
My flat is smaller than yours.
The more you practise, the better you speak.
examples.note: The ... the ... shows two things that change together.

mistakes.wrong: She is more taller than me.
It is the more expensive hotel in town.
mistakes.right: It is the most expensive hotel in town.

mistakes.wrong: He is the taller of the group.
mistakes.right: He is the tallest in the group.
mistakes.why: Use the superlative for three or more.

checks.question: Complete: Mount Everest is ___ (high) mountain in the world.
Complete: This exercise is ___ (difficult) than the last one.

sections.title: Modifying comparatives
sections.summary: Add a word before a comparative to say how big the difference is.

tables.caption: Words before a comparative
head: size of difference
words
example
rows: much, a lot, far, a great deal
Her house is much bigger than mine.
a bit, a little, slightly, a little bit
He is as tall as his father.
nearly as ... as, not quite as ... as
I am not quite as fast as him.

uses: Use much, a lot or far for a big difference: far better, much more expensive.
Use a bit or slightly for a small difference.
Do not use very before a comparative: very better is wrong. Use much better.
Use by + a number for exact differences: He is taller by two centimetres.

examples.text: The new phone is a lot faster than my old one.
Today is slightly warmer than yesterday.
This test was nowhere near as hard as the last one.
examples.note: Nowhere near as = much less than.

mistakes.why: Do not use very with a comparative.

mistakes.wrong: The film was too better than the book.
mistakes.right: The film was far better than the book.
mistakes.why: Use far, much or a lot.

checks.question: Choose: This chair is (very / much) more comfortable.
Choose: This coat is (a lot / a bit) cheaper than that one: it costs only two pounds less.

sections.title: Gradable and non-gradable adjectives
sections.summary: Gradable adjectives have degrees (a bit cold, very cold). Non-gradable adjectives are extreme or absolute and need other adverbs.
uses: Use very, quite, extremely and a bit with gradable adjectives.
Use absolutely, completely, totally and utterly with extreme adjectives.
Do not say very freezing or very exhausted.
Really works with both types: really cold, really freezing.
Some adjectives are non-gradable because they are absolute: perfect, unique, impossible, dead.

examples.text: I am very tired after the trip.
It is quite good, but not fantastic.
examples.note: Quite goes with gradable adjectives; fantastic is extreme.

checks.question: Choose: The view was (very / absolutely) amazing.
